stem: A 58-year-old man has 6 months of intermittent right arm numbness and pain. Imaging shows a complete right cervical rib compressing the brachial plexus, and removal of the rib is planned.
oneliner: 58M + right arm numbness + complete right cervical rib compressing the brachial plexus + rib removal → which vessel at risk?
ask: Which vessel is at greatest risk during removal of the rib?

whyNot.A: Lies **proximal**, in the mediastinum behind the manubrium, away from a **cervical rib**
whyNot.C: Ascends to the **skull base**, far from a **cervical rib**
whyNot.D: Runs up the neck in the carotid sheath, **medial** to the scalenes and away from the rib
whyNot.E: Leaves the subclavian and climbs into the **transverse foramina**, away from the rib

why: The **subclavian artery** and **brachial plexus** pass over the **first rib between the anterior and middle scalenes**, exactly where a **cervical rib** compresses them. Resection puts the **subclavian artery** at risk.

idea.rule: Subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass between the scalenes; the subclavian vein passes in front.
also: Subclavian vein runs anterior to the anterior scalene
Thoracic outlet syndrome causes neurogenic or vascular symptoms
Cervical rib arises from C7

stem: A 42-year-old man falls from a ladder and fractures his humerus. Afterward he cannot extend his wrist or fingers, and he has numbness over the back of the first web space of his hand.
oneliner: 42M + fall + humerus fracture + cannot extend wrist and fingers + numb dorsal first web space → which fracture site?
ask: Which fracture site most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.B: The **axillary nerve** runs here and gives shoulder **abduction weakness** with numb lateral upper arm, not wrist drop
whyNot.C: The **ulnar nerve** passes behind this point: **clawing** of the ring and little fingers, not wrist drop
whyNot.D: The nerve most at risk here is the **median** (often its anterior interosseous branch): weak thumb and index flexion and lateral palm numbness, not wrist drop
whyNot.E: An avulsion of the **rotator cuff** insertion that weakens shoulder abduction and rotation, without nerve loss in the **wrist and hand**

answer: Mid-shaft fracture at the radial (spiral) groove, injuring the radial nerve
why: The **radial nerve** winds around the humerus in the **spiral groove**, so a **mid-shaft fracture** injures it. This paralyses the **wrist and finger extensors** (**wrist drop**) and causes **sensory loss over the dorsal first web space**.

idea.rule: Mid-shaft humerus fracture = radial nerve; surgical neck = axillary; medial epicondyle = ulnar; supracondylar = median.
also: Triceps is often spared because its branches leave before the groove
Saturday night palsy: radial nerve compression in the axilla or arm
Radial neck fracture: posterior interosseous nerve injury gives finger drop without sensory loss

stem: A 22-year-old man falls on his outstretched hand. He is tender in the hollow on the radial side of the wrist between the tendons at the base of the thumb, and the radial pulse can be felt in the hollow. His first wrist x-ray is normal.
oneliner: 22M + fall on outstretched hand + tender hollow at radial wrist + radial pulse in it + normal first x-ray → which bone lies in the floor?
ask: Which carpal bone forms the floor of the tender area?

whyNot.A: Lies in the **center** of the proximal row, not in the floor of the **radial hollow** where the pulse is felt
whyNot.C: Sits on the **ulnar** side as a sesamoid in flexor carpi ulnaris, far from the **radial hollow**
whyNot.D: Projects from the **ulnar** side of the palm and is injured by a **racquet or club**, not a fall on the radial wrist
whyNot.E: The largest carpal bone lies in the **center** of the wrist, deep to the middle finger, not in the **radial hollow**

why: The **anatomic snuffbox** is bounded by the tendons of **abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis** laterally and **extensor pollicis longus** medially, with the **radial artery** crossing its floor. The **scaphoid** forms the floor, and **tenderness here after a fall with a normal first film** suggests a **scaphoid fracture**.

idea.rule: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the hand is a scaphoid fracture until proved otherwise, even with a normal first film.
also: Scaphoid fractures can cause avascular necrosis of the proximal pole because blood supply enters distally
Initial x-rays may be negative; repeat films or MRI
Radial artery crosses the snuffbox floor

stem: A 30-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand. She has central pain on the palm side of the wrist and numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers. There is no tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb.
oneliner: 30F + fall on outstretched hand + central palm-side wrist pain + numb thumb, index, middle fingers + no snuffbox tenderness → which bone and nerve?
ask: Which bone is most likely displaced and which nerve is compressed?

options.A: Scaphoid, with the superficial radial nerve
options.C: Hook of hamate, with the ulnar nerve

whyNot.A: Scaphoid injury gives **snuffbox tenderness**, which she lacks, and superficial radial injury causes **dorsal** hand numbness
whyNot.C: The hook of the hamate lies on the **ulnar** side and the ulnar nerve supplies the **ring and little fingers**, not hers
whyNot.D: The pisiform is an **ulnar** sesamoid, and the ulnar nerve does not supply the **thumb, index and middle** fingers
whyNot.E: The trapezoid is a **distal row** bone that is rarely dislocated and does not explain the **central** pain; the lunate lies at the **center** of the proximal row

answer: Lunate (anterior dislocation), compressing the median nerve
why: The **lunate**, the central bone of the proximal row, dislocates **anteriorly** into the **carpal tunnel** after a fall on the hand. It compresses the **median nerve**, causing numbness of the **lateral three digits**, with **central volar pain** and **no snuffbox tenderness**.

idea.rule: Lunate dislocates volar into the carpal tunnel and compresses the median nerve.
also: In perilunate dislocation the capitate displaces dorsally while the lunate stays with the radius
Carpal tunnel contents: median nerve and nine flexor tendons
Spilled teacup sign on lateral x-ray

stem: A 24-year-old woman has numbness along the medial forearm and hand and weakness of the small muscles of the hand. Symptoms worsen when she holds her arm overhead. A chest film shows an extra rib arising from the seventh cervical vertebra.
oneliner: 24F + numb medial forearm and hand + weak small hand muscles + worse with arm overhead + cervical rib on x-ray → which plexus part?
ask: Which part of the brachial plexus is most likely compressed?

options.A: Upper trunk, roots C5 and C6

whyNot.A: Upper trunk injury (Erb) gives **shoulder abduction and elbow flexion weakness**, not hand weakness
whyNot.B: The posterior cord gives the **axillary and radial** nerves, with **wrist drop**, not medial hand numbness
whyNot.C: The lateral cord gives the **musculocutaneous nerve** and lateral median root, causing weak elbow flexion and **lateral forearm** numbness
whyNot.E: Middle trunk (C7) carries **triceps and wrist extensors** and sensation to the middle finger, not the **medial hand**

why: A **cervical rib** crowds the thoracic outlet and presses on the **lower trunk (C8-T1)** as it arches over the first rib. This causes **medial forearm and hand sensory loss** and **intrinsic hand weakness** (Klumpke-like), often with subclavian vessel compression.

idea.rule: Lower trunk (C8-T1) injury or compression affects the ulnar-side hand and intrinsic muscles.
also: Klumpke palsy: lower trunk avulsion, claw hand and Horner syndrome
Pancoast tumor can also compress the lower trunk
Subclavian artery compression gives a pale cool hand and diminished pulse

stem: A 19-year-old man playing softball caught his ring finger in an opponent's jersey while gripping, and now cannot bend the tip of that finger. When the examiner holds the middle joint of the finger straight, he cannot flex the end joint at all, but the middle joint flexes normally when released. Sensation is normal.
oneliner: 19M + softball + finger caught in jersey + cannot flex fingertip with PIP held straight + PIP flexion intact + normal sensation → which tendon?
ask: Disruption of which structure best explains this finding?

whyNot.A: Inserts on the **middle phalanx** and flexes the PIP joint, which is **intact** here
whyNot.B: Would cause weak **extension**, not loss of fingertip flexion
whyNot.D: Flexes the **thumb** interphalangeal joint, not the ring finger
whyNot.E: An **index finger** extensor; no flexion role

answer: Flexor digitorum profundus tendon avulsion from the distal phalanx
why: **FDP** inserts on the **distal phalanx** and is the **only flexor of the DIP joint**, so its avulsion leaves **PIP flexion intact** (FDS) with the fingertip unable to bend. Sensation is normal because this is a tendon, not a nerve, injury.

idea.rule: DIP flexion = FDP only; PIP flexion = FDS (and FDP helps).
also: Jersey finger = FDP avulsion, classically the ring finger
FDS inserts on the sides of the middle phalanx
Mallet finger is the opposite: extensor tendon avulsion at the DIP

stem: A 44-year-old man with a forearm fracture is unable to make a circle with his thumb and index finger; when he tries, the end joints stay straight and the pads do not touch. Flexing the ring and little fingertips is normal, and he has no numbness anywhere in the hand.
oneliner: 44M + forearm fracture + cannot make OK sign (index DIP and thumb IP straight) + ring and little DIP flexion normal + no numbness → which nerve?
ask: Which nerve is most likely injured?

whyNot.A: Supplies FDP to digits **4-5**, which flex normally; ulnar injury would also cause sensory loss
whyNot.C: Supplies the **extensors**, so its loss weakens extension; the deficit here is fingertip **flexion**
whyNot.D: A **radial** branch to extensors; it does not supply flexors
whyNot.E: Acts on elbow flexion; it does not reach the **forearm flexors of the fingers**

answer: Anterior interosseous nerve (branch of the median nerve)
why: The **anterior interosseous nerve** supplies **FDP to digits 2-3**, **flexor pollicis longus** and **pronator quadratus**, with **no skin branch**, so there is weakness without numbness. Digits 4-5 of FDP come from the **ulnar nerve**, which explains their normal flexion.

idea.rule: Anterior interosseous nerve = pure motor: FPL, lateral FDP, pronator quadratus.
also: Supracondylar fracture is a classic cause
Median nerve proper injury also causes thenar weakness and sensory loss
FDP is dual-innervated: median (digits 2-3), ulnar (digits 4-5)

stem: A 52-year-old male electrician has had neck pain with grip weakness for 3 weeks. Finger flexion is weak, but finger extension and elbow extension are normal. The finger flexor reflex is reduced, and there is numbness of the little finger and the inner border of the hand.
oneliner: 52M + neck pain + weak grip + normal finger and elbow extension + reduced finger flexor reflex + numb little finger and medial hand → which root?
ask: Which nerve root is most likely compressed?

whyNot.A: Gives wrist extension and the **biceps** reflex; its numbness is over the **thumb**, not the little finger
whyNot.B: Controls **finger and elbow extension** (triceps), which are normal here
whyNot.C: Mainly finger **abduction**; its skin is the **medial forearm and arm**, not the little finger
whyNot.E: Shoulder abduction and **deltoid**; its numbness is over the lateral arm, not the little finger

why: Finger flexion and the finger flexor reflex are mainly **C8**, and the **little finger and medial hand** are its skin territory. **C7** drives finger and elbow extension, which are normal, and **T1** supplies the medial forearm and abducts the fingers.

idea.rule: C7 extends, C8 flexes the fingers, T1 spreads them.
also: C5: shoulder abduction, deltoid
C6: wrist extension, biceps reflex, thumb
C7: elbow extension, triceps reflex, middle finger numbness

stem: A 48-year-old woman has trouble crossing her legs and walks with her right leg swinging outward since pelvic lymph node surgery. She has numbness over the inner right thigh, and extending the knee against resistance is normal.
oneliner: 48F + pelvic surgery + right leg swings outward when walking + inner thigh numbness + normal knee extension → which movement is weak?
ask: Which movement is most likely weak?

whyNot.B: Gluteus medius and minimus (**superior gluteal nerve**); weakness gives a Trendelenburg gait, not inner-thigh numbness
whyNot.C: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris, mostly **femoral nerve**, which also extends the knee (**normal** here)
whyNot.D: Gluteus maximus (**inferior gluteal nerve**); trouble rising from a chair or climbing stairs
whyNot.E: Done mainly by small **sacral plexus** rotators; their loss would not explain inner-thigh numbness or trouble crossing the legs

why: The **obturator nerve** passes through the **obturator foramen** to supply the **medial (adductor) compartment** and a patch of **medial thigh skin**. Weak adductors leave the abductors unopposed, so the leg **circumducts**.

idea.rule: Obturator nerve = adductors and medial thigh skin.
also: Pelvic surgery, lateral pelvic wall hernia (obturator hernia) can injure it
Femoral nerve (L2-L4) supplies the anterior thigh and extends the knee
Superior gluteal nerve injury gives Trendelenburg sign

stem: A 24-year-old male sprinter feels a pop high in the inner thigh during a start and now has pain and weakness when squeezing his knees together. MRI shows a tear of the largest adductor muscle, which inserts along the back of the femur down to a tubercle above the medial condyle. The tear is in its vertical fibres, which also work with the hamstrings to extend the hip.
oneliner: 24M + sprinter + inner thigh pop + weak hip adduction + tear of largest adductor's vertical fibres that help the hamstrings extend the hip → which origin?
ask: From which bony site do the torn fibres arise?

whyNot.A: Origin of **rectus femoris**, a hip flexor and knee extensor, not an adductor
whyNot.B: Gives origin to **abdominal wall** muscles, not to an adductor that inserts on the femur
whyNot.D: Origin of **piriformis**, a lateral rotator, not an adductor
whyNot.E: Origin of the **gluteal** muscles, which abduct or extend; they do not adduct

answer: Ischial tuberosity (hamstring part of adductor magnus)
why: **Adductor magnus** is the largest adductor; its adductor part arises from the **ischiopubic ramus** and its vertical **hamstring part** from the **ischial tuberosity**, inserting on the **linea aspera** and **adductor tubercle**. That hamstring part extends the hip and is supplied by the **tibial part of the sciatic nerve**.

idea.rule: Adductors arise from the pubis/ischium and insert on the femur; the obturator nerve supplies most of them.
also: Adductor longus and brevis arise from the pubis
Gracilis arises from the pubis and inserts on the tibia
Adductor part of adductor magnus is supplied by the obturator nerve

stem: A 37-year-old male cyclist has deep buttock pain after long rides that worsens when sitting. Turning the thigh outward against resistance reproduces the pain, and the examiner finds weakness of that movement. Imaging shows a tight muscle crossing just above the sciatic nerve as it leaves the pelvis.
oneliner: 37M + cyclist + deep buttock pain worse sitting + weak lateral rotation + tight muscle above sciatic nerve exit → which muscle?
ask: Which muscle is most likely involved?

whyNot.A: Abducts and **medially rotates** the thigh, the opposite of the weak movement
whyNot.C: An **anterior thigh** adductor and hip flexor
whyNot.D: Runs on the **medial thigh** and adducts; it is not in the buttock
whyNot.E: Anterior thigh muscle that **flexes the hip** and extends the knee

why: **Piriformis** is a **lateral rotator** of the thigh in the buttock, and the **sciatic nerve** usually passes just below it, which explains the buttock pain pattern. **Gluteus minimus** is the opposing **medial rotator** and abductor.

idea.rule: Lateral rotators of the hip: piriformis, obturators, gemelli, quadratus femoris.
also: Gluteus medius and minimus abduct and medially rotate
Piriformis syndrome mimics sciatica
Piriformis arises from the anterior sacrum

stem: A 40-year-old man who works as a mover felt a pop in the low back while lifting a heavy box. He now has pain shooting down the back of the leg to the outer edge of the foot, with weak plantar flexion and an absent ankle jerk. MRI shows a posterolateral herniation at the lowest lumbar disc space.
oneliner: 40M + lifting injury + pain to lateral foot + weak plantar flexion + absent ankle jerk + posterolateral L5-S1 herniation on MRI → which root?
ask: Which nerve root is most likely compressed?

whyNot.A: Exits through the foramen **above** this disc, so a posterolateral herniation spares it; L5 loss keeps the ankle jerk
whyNot.B: Would reduce the **patellar reflex** and numb the medial leg, not the outer foot
whyNot.C: Exits lower in the sacrum; its skin is the **back of the thigh**, not the outer edge of the foot
whyNot.E: Gives anterior thigh symptoms and a reduced **patellar reflex**, not an absent ankle jerk

why: A **posterolateral** lumbar herniation compresses the **root that exits below that disc**; for the **L5-S1** disc that is the **S1 root**. S1 gives **plantar flexion**, the **ankle jerk** and **lateral foot** sensation.

idea.rule: Posterolateral disc compresses the root of the level below (traversing root).
also: L4-L5 herniation compresses L5: weak great-toe extension, footdrop
L3-L4 herniation compresses L4: reduced patellar reflex
Central herniation at L4-L5 can cause cauda equina syndrome

stem: A 55-year-old woman has back pain and a left footdrop. A myelogram shows disc material bulging backward into the spinal canal to one side of the midline instead of straight back. The surgeon explains that a ligament covering the back of the disc is strong in the midline but thin at its edges.
oneliner: 55F + back pain + footdrop + disc bulging into canal off midline + ligament behind disc strong centrally, thin laterally → which ligament?
ask: Weakness of which ligament at its edges explains the direction of herniation?

whyNot.A: Joins adjacent **laminae** on the back wall of the canal, not over the disc
whyNot.B: Lies on the **front** of the bodies and discs, away from the canal the disc bulged into
whyNot.C: Connects **spinous processes**, behind the canal, not over the disc
whyNot.D: Runs along the **spinous process tips**, far from the disc

why: The **posterior longitudinal ligament** runs on the **back of the vertebral bodies and discs inside the canal**. It is strong in the midline and **thin laterally**, so the nucleus pulposus herniates **posterolaterally** into the intervertebral foramen.

idea.rule: Disc herniation direction follows the weak point of the posterior longitudinal ligament.
also: Ligamentum flavum thickening contributes to spinal stenosis
Anterior longitudinal ligament limits extension
Nucleus pulposus is the embryonic notochord remnant

stem: A 27-year-old male climber lands awkwardly after a fall and cannot bear weight. Swelling is present on both sides of the ankle. X-ray shows a small bone fragment pulled off the medial malleolus together with a fracture of the distal fibula.
oneliner: 27M + climbing fall + swelling both sides of ankle + avulsed medial malleolus + distal fibular fracture → which force?
ask: Which forced position most likely caused this injury?

whyNot.B: Tears the **lateral** ligaments (anterior talofibular first) or avulses the lateral malleolus
whyNot.C: Jams the talus into the mortise; it does not pull a fragment off the **medial malleolus**
whyNot.D: Loads the **lateral** ligaments when combined with inversion; it does not avulse the medial malleolus
whyNot.E: Produces a **pilon** (tibial plafond) fracture, with crushing, not a medial avulsion

why: Forced **eversion** tears the strong **deltoid ligament** or **avulses the medial malleolus**, while the talus pushes the **fibula** laterally and fractures it. Inversion does the opposite, injuring the weaker **lateral** ligaments.

idea.rule: Eversion injures the medial side (deltoid) and may fracture the fibula; inversion injures the lateral side.
also: Inversion sprain: anterior talofibular ligament is the most commonly torn
Maisonneuve fracture involves the proximal fibula and syndesmosis
Deltoid ligament is stronger than lateral ligaments

stem: A 33-year-old woman yawned widely during a long meeting and now cannot close her mouth. Her chin is displaced forward and the jaw is fixed open. Examination shows both mandibular condyles sitting in front of the articular eminence.
oneliner: 33F + wide yawn + cannot close mouth + jaw locked open + condyles anterior to articular eminence → which muscle pulled the condyle forward?
ask: Contraction of which muscle most directly pulled the condyle forward?

whyNot.A: **Elevates** the mandible and closes the jaw; it does not protrude it
whyNot.C: **Elevates** the mandible and helps lateral movement
whyNot.E: A **cheek** muscle that holds food between the teeth, no role in jaw opening

answer: Lateral pterygoid, which protrudes and depresses the mandible
why: The **lateral pterygoid** pulls the **condyle and disc forward** onto the articular eminence, protruding the mandible and starting jaw opening; overpull carries the condyle in front of the eminence. **Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid** are elevators whose spasm then holds the jaw locked.

idea.rule: Lateral pterygoid protrudes and opens the jaw; masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid close it.
also: Lateral pterygoid is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3)
Mandibular dislocation is usually anterior
Anterior belly of digastric and mylohyoid also help depress the mandible

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought in crying after her father pulled her up by the hand to stop her from falling. She now holds her arm slightly bent at her side with the forearm turned palm down and refuses to use it. The elbow is not swollen and an x-ray is normal.
oneliner: 2F + pulled up by the hand + arm held flexed and pronated + refuses to use arm + normal x-ray → which ligament?
ask: Which ligament is involved in this injury?

whyNot.A: Stabilises the **medial elbow** against valgus force; injured in throwers
whyNot.B: Stabilises the **lateral elbow** against varus force
whyNot.D: Joins the **radius and ulna shafts**; it does not hold the radial head in place
whyNot.E: A short band from the ulna to the **radial neck**; the radial head slips out of the annular ring, not this band

answer: Annular ligament, with subluxation of the radial head
why: The **annular ligament** wraps the **radial head** against the ulna. In toddlers it is **lax**, so a sudden **longitudinal pull** slips the head through it (**nursemaid elbow**) and the child holds the arm **pronated and flexed**.

idea.rule: Annular ligament holds the radial head; a toddler's pulled arm subluxes it.
also: Treatment is hyperpronation or supination with flexion
X-ray is normal
Nursemaid elbow usually occurs at ages 1-4

stem: A 19-year-old male driver is brought in after a head-on crash where his flexed knee struck the dashboard. With the knee bent to 90 degrees, the examiner can pull the upper tibia backward more than on the other side. Anterior drawer, Lachman, and varus and valgus stress tests are all normal.
oneliner: 19M + dashboard knee strike + excess backward tibial translation at 90 degrees + normal anterior drawer, Lachman, varus and valgus tests → which structure?
ask: Which structure is most likely torn?

whyNot.A: Limits **anterior** tibial translation; Lachman and anterior drawer would be positive
whyNot.C: Opposes **valgus** stress, which is normal here
whyNot.D: Opposes **varus** stress, which is normal here
whyNot.E: Causes **joint line pain** and locking, not excess posterior translation

why: The **PCL** runs from the **medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibia** and prevents **posterior tibial translation**, so a torn PCL gives a **positive posterior drawer**. A **dashboard injury** drives the flexed tibia backward.

idea.rule: ACL stops the tibia sliding forward; PCL stops it sliding back.
also: Dashboard injury or fall on a flexed knee tears the PCL
ACL injury: pivoting, pop, positive Lachman
Unhappy triad: ACL, MCL and medial meniscus
